prompt: Review the Checkout Service extraction proposal in docs/design/checkout-service-extraction.md and the supporting packet around it. I own the architecture decision and need to know whether this design is safe to approve for implementation now. Check the proposal's claims against the supporting material and the constraints it cites. Focus on concrete risks that could change the approval decision, cause customer impact after launch, or rest on assumptions the packet does not support. Write the review to REVIEW.md at the top of the project. End it with a fenced json list of findings, each with location (the section number of the document, like 3.2), severity (critical, high, medium, low or nit), issue and fix.

checks.cmd: node -e 'const fs=require("fs");const t=fs.readFileSync("REVIEW.md","utf8");let L=null;for(const m of t.matchAll(/^\x60\x60\x60([a-z]*)[ \t]*\n([\s\S]*?)^\x60\x60\x60[ \t]*$/gim)){if(m[1]&&m[1].toLowerCase()!=="json")continue;let d;try{d=JSON.parse(m[2])}catch{continue}const l=Array.isArray(d)?d:Array.isArray(d&&d.findings)?d.findings:null;if(l&&l.every(x=>x&&typeof x==="object"&&!Array.isArray(x))){L=l;break}}if(!L||!L.length)process.exit(1);const S=["critical","high","medium","low","nit"];process.exit(L.every(x=>x.location&&S.includes(String(x.severity).toLowerCase())&&(x.issue||x.fix||x.text))?0:1)'

node -e 'const fs=require("fs");const t=fs.readFileSync("REVIEW.md","utf8");let L=null;for(const m of t.matchAll(/^\x60\x60\x60([a-z]*)[ \t]*\n([\s\S]*?)^\x60\x60\x60[ \t]*$/gim)){if(m[1]&&m[1].toLowerCase()!=="json")continue;let d;try{d=JSON.parse(m[2])}catch{continue}const l=Array.isArray(d)?d:Array.isArray(d&&d.findings)?d.findings:null;if(l&&l.every(x=>x&&typeof x==="object"&&!Array.isArray(x))){L=l;break}}if(!L||!L.length)process.exit(1);const H=new Set();for(const l of fs.readFileSync("docs/design/checkout-service-extraction.md","utf8").split("\n")){const m=l.match(/^#+\s*(?:section\s*)?(\d+(?:\.\d+)*)/i);if(m)H.add(m[1])}process.exit(L.every(x=>{const m=String(x.location).match(/\d+(?:\.\d+)*/);return m&&H.has(m[0])})?0:1)'

rubric.criterion: Each important finding explains the concrete consequence in this project and gives a fix a developer can act on, without inventing problems unsupported by the packet. Fail: generic findings ("add validation", "consider security"), or a finding the packet does not support. Partial: findings are grounded in the packet but some lack an actionable fix or a concrete consequence. Pass: every important finding names the place, the concrete consequence in this project and a fix a developer can build, and no finding is invented. (code cannot check this because it requires judging the review's meaning against the project context).

findingsKey.finding: The extracted service still writes the monolith's Order Platform, Payments, and Fulfillment tables directly, so the proposed boundary leaves shared storage ownership and coupling unchanged.

Payment authorization, inventory reservation, and order creation are separate operations without a defined compensation or recovery contract when a later step fails, leaving partial charges or reservations possible.
The stated 440 ms total ignores the context's p99 timings for the three serial network hops and exceeds the 450 ms checkout budget once those measurements are used.
The rollout changes the primary path by percentage but never runs both implementations on the same requests and compares their outcomes before increasing customer traffic.
Customer table ownership and the permitted writer remain undecided even though the service caches and reads legacy profile data, so launch authority and future schema changes are unclear.

The listed subscription, returns, support, partner, and worker callers have only a vague promise of an adapter and later migration, with no per-caller contract, owner, or retirement path for the monolith interface.

The retry design reuses a local payment attempt ID but does not send the provider idempotency key or durably record the provider request before retrying, repeating the duplicate-authorization failure described in the incident.

items.text: Asks how the service sheds load when Payments or Fulfillment slows down, what is rejected first, and how pending work is bounded.
Checks that service identities, issuer and audience claims, and propagated customer claims are validated so a caller cannot substitute an arbitrary identity.
items.source: RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700 (IETF Trust Legal Provisions)

items.text: Checks that configuration, database credentials, and provider settings are injected at runtime rather than coupled to the service artifact.
Asks whether logs, traces, support search, and retained state have an explicit access policy and retention test for customer data and operational identifiers.
items.source: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series, https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org (CC BY-SA 4.0)

items.text: Requests evidence that a zone loss, dependency outage, or reconciliation backlog stays within the availability objective with bounded recovery and enough capacity.
Asks who owns the public SLO and error-budget decision when rollout signals disagree across regions or callers.

weakAnswers: The proposal is clear and the staged rollout looks sensible.
Consider scalability, monitoring, and future growth before implementation.
The service boundary and API design seem reasonable; add more tests.
The document covers performance, reliability, security, and operations well.

verdicts.note: The prompt asks for a design review without naming a specific method, checklist, process, or hinting at planted problems. It does not state how many issues exist.

The task clearly specifies reviewing the proposal against supporting material, focusing on concrete risks, writing findings to REVIEW.md, and formatting them as a JSON list with location (section number), severity, issue, and fix.

The key items require cross-referencing claims in the proposal against numbers and constraints in service-targets.yaml, data-ownership.md, incident-2024-11.md, and checkout-call-graph.csv. A shallow read that only looks at the design document would miss most findings.

All key items are grounded in the fixture: k1 matches section 3.2 and data-ownership.md; k2 matches section 3.4 workflow description; k3's math is verifiable in service-targets.yaml; k4 matches section 5.1 rollout text; k5 matches section 3.3 customer arrangement text; k6 matches section 2.3 caller list; k7 matches section 6.3 and incident-2024-11.md. Severities are defensible.

No comments, tests, docs, or file names point at the planted problems. The incident summary describes a past failure that the proposal repeats, but it is legitimate supporting context, not a hidden answer.
